title: E-Values Evaluating the Values of AI: Sheila Gulati and Nischal Nadhamuni

Klarity operates in enterprise document automation with Finance and Accounting workflows, while the evaluation methodology discussion applies broadly across domains. summary: Sheila Gulati (Tola Capital founder) and Nischal Nadhamuni (Klarity CTO/co-founder) present on AI evaluations at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Sheila frames evals as a seminal concern as AI moves toward agentic, self-learning systems. She compares the cloud era—where evaluation focused on performance, functionality, and price of physical infrastructure—to the AI era, which shares large capex and mega-cap participation but adds open-source model proliferation, deep academic heritage, and complex agentic automation. She stresses AI reflects human values and society, making broad AI evaluation multifaceted across capability, domain, values, safety, context, end-user awareness, and modality. Current eval tools suffer from benchmark hacking, weak real-world generalization (FinanceBench), absent end-user focus, black-box opacity, and unresolved value-alignment questions. Sheila raises echo chamber concerns and asks whether AI should appease or challenge users, ground in present or aspirational values, and who bears responsibility for embedded values. Nischal grounds the discussion in Klarity's eight-year journey automating document-centric back-office workflows. Founded in 2016, Klarity pivoted four times before finding product-market fit in Finance and Accounting, then re-platformed around generative AI. They now process over 500,000 documents with 15+ unique LLM use cases and 10+ LLMs in production. He explains why generative AI evaluation differs from traditional ML across non-deterministic performance on cognitively demanding tasks, novel user experiences resisting simple metrics, and accelerated feature development cycles making eval the bottleneck. He offers practical strategies: give yourself the gift of imperfection by not requiring high-quality evals upfront; frontload UX testing and backload evals since many features die at the UX stage; think backward from user experience; build per-customer annotated data and use-case-specific accuracy metrics; avoid assuming absence of user feedback is positive; invest in data drift monitoring; and build custom synthetic data generation after surveying six-plus commercial providers. He adds two further strategies: reduce degrees of freedom by standardizing on one LLM for automated prompt engineering tasks across 100+ customers rather than running exponential grid searches, trading marginal accuracy for iteration speed; and build scrappy future-facing evals to develop organizational mental models quickly—such as evaluating GPT-V within an hour of release. Sheila closes with a community call to action: reinvent benchmarks rather than accepting leaderboard BS, bring depth and multifaceted evaluation as a community, share openly, introspect value systems, and recognize that those early to the AI revolution bear disproportionate responsibility. She references The Alignment Problem and the idea that AGI will be a mirror of society, telling us which values are uniquely human.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Evals are urgent as AI becomes agentic and self-sufficient; narrow-AI evaluation methods no longer suffice across capability, domain, values, safety, context, and modality.

Benchmark hacking is rampant; dynamic benchmarks with non-public synthetic data address memorization, and real-world generalization gaps persist (FinanceBench showed MMLU-strong models failing basic financial questions).
Values are inevitably embedded in models—echo chambers and polarization raise unresolved questions about appeasing vs. challenging users and grounding AI in present vs. aspirational values.

Generative AI eval differs from traditional ML: non-determinism on cognitive tasks, novel UX resistive to simple metrics, feature cycles in days (not months) making eval the bottleneck, and benchmark scores diverging from real performance.
Frontload UX testing and backload evals; many features die at the UX stage—let them die before investing in evals.
Reduce degrees of freedom by standardizing on one LLM for automated prompt engineering tasks across customers rather than running expensive grid searches; trade marginal accuracy for iteration speed.
Build scrappy future-facing evals to develop organizational mental models quickly—evaluate new models within hours of release rather than waiting for formal benchmark-grade metrics.
Reinvent benchmarks as a community; do not let leaderboard benchmarks that lack genuine understanding stick; share journeys openly and introspect value systems as trailblazers.
Understand why AI evaluation is at a seminal moment as systems become agentic and self-sufficient
Identify multifaceted dimensions of broad AI evaluation: capability, domain, values, safety, context, end-user awareness, modality

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Context
sections.summary: Sheila introduces herself and Nischal as an investor-investee pair. Klarity automates document-centric workflows and just announced a $70M Series B. Sheila founded Tola Capital after helping launch Microsoft Azure, framing the firm around next-generation cloud and now AI applications.

sections.title: From Cloud to AI: Scale, Proliferation, and Values
sections.summary: Sheila compares cloud-era evaluation (performance, functionality, price of physical infrastructure) to the AI era, which shares large capex and mega-cap participation but adds open-source model proliferation and academic heritage. She stresses AI reflects human values and society, especially as agents represent individuals.

sections.title: AI Evolution and the Urgency of Evals
sections.summary: AI evolved from consuming internet data through emergent behaviors and curated datasets toward self-taught, self-sufficient models. Evals must be fixed before full automation. Narrow AI eval was straightforward; broad AI eval is multifaceted across capability, domain, values, safety, context, end-user awareness, and modality.

sections.title: Limitations of Current Eval Methods
sections.summary: Sheila details benchmark hacking (solve for X), dynamic benchmarks as a fix (Microsoft research), benchmarks vs. real-world gaps (FinanceBench), absent end-user/UX evaluation, black-box opacity requiring interpretability research, and unresolved questions about values instilled in models for an agentic world.

sections.title: Value Questions and Transition to Klarity
sections.summary: Sheila raises echo chamber concerns—AI reflecting its makers' beliefs deepens polarization. She poses open questions: should AI appease or challenge users, ground in present or aspirational values, allow user value selection, and who bears responsibility. She then introduces Nischal to share Klarity's real-world eval journey.

sections.title: Klarity's Background and Journey
sections.summary: Nischal introduces Klarity, automating document-centric back-office workflows (e.g., revenue recognition, invoice-to-PO matching, tax withholdings). Founded in 2016, the company pivoted four times before finding product-market fit in Finance and Accounting, then re-platformed around generative AI after six years in traditional ML. They now process 500K+ documents with 15+ LLM use cases and 10+ LLMs in production, having raised $90M+.

sections.title: Why GenAI Eval Differs from Traditional ML
sections.summary: Nischal explains three key differences: non-deterministic performance on cognitively demanding tasks, novel user experiences (Architect workflow recorder, natural-language analytics, document extraction) that resist simple metrics, and accelerated feature cycles (days vs. months) making eval the bottleneck. He also confirms benchmark divergence—models with higher MMLU sometimes perform worse on internal benchmarks.

sections.title: Practical Eval Strategies at Klarity
sections.summary: Nischal shares strategies: give yourself the gift of imperfection—don't require high-quality evals upfront; frontload UX testing and backload evals since many features die at UX stage; think backward from user experience, walking down the stack from outcomes to health metrics; build per-customer annotated data with use-case-specific accuracy metrics; don't assume absence of user feedback is positive; monitor data drift; and invest in custom synthetic data generation after surveying six-plus providers, with teams monitoring distributional similarity for customer-agnostic evals.

sections.title: Reducing Complexity and Future-Facing Evals
sections.summary: Nischal describes reducing degrees of freedom by standardizing on one LLM for automated prompt engineering tasks across 100+ customers, trading marginal accuracy for iteration speed rather than building expensive grid-search infrastructure. He also advocates building scrappy future-facing evals—such as evaluating GPT-V within an hour of release with a mental model of its strengths (good at checkmarks, not pie charts)—to develop organizational intuition quickly. He closes with a hiring plug across AI, backend, frontend, and go-to-market roles after the $70M Series B.

sections.title: Sheila's Closing Call to Action
sections.summary: Sheila closes with a community call to action. Early AI adopters matter disproportionately and bear responsibility for integrating values into next-generation evals. She urges reinventing benchmarks rather than accepting leaderboard benchmarks that lack genuine understanding, bringing depth and multifaceted evaluation as a community, sharing journeys openly, and introspecting personal value systems. She references The Alignment Problem and the idea that AGI will be a mirror of society, revealing which values are uniquely human. She calls on attendees to feel empowered, be curious, stay empathetic, kind, fair, and intelligent—framing the work as printing new intelligence for the world, both opportunity and accountability.

limitations: Benchmark hacking: models score high on known benchmarks without genuine understanding
Benchmarks vs. real-world scenarios: models claiming generalizability fail specific reasoning questions
End users are often afterthoughts in evaluation; UX evaluation is difficult
Black-box models: evaluation is a proxy for truth, not truth itself; neural network learning is not mathematically representable
Non-deterministic performance makes GenAI eval challenging for cognitively demanding tasks
Novel generative experiences (workflow recording, NL analytics) resist simple evaluation metrics
Accelerated feature development (days) makes eval the bottleneck if it takes weeks
Benchmark scores (e.g., MMLU) diverge from real-world task performance
Absence of user feedback should not be assumed to be positive feedback
Fully automated quantitative synthetic data evaluation remains unsolved
Exponential complexity explosion when combining multiple LLMs across multiple customers and features makes full grid search impractical
